1 Preface: why this manual exists
This document is a self-contained mathematical companion to the doctoral thesis The Resonating Self. A
Resonance Theory of Consciousness (RTC). In several places the thesis relies on differential and integral
calculus and on nonlinear dynamics — most notably in Chapter 4 (the Psychophysical Time Quantum and
Mind-Energy) and Chapter 9 (the Mathematical Formalism). For readers without an extensive mathematical
background, and for examiners who wish to check the formal underpinnings step by step, a separate and
thorough exposition is desirable. That exposition is given here.
The manual carries one guiding thread that distinguishes it from any standard calculus textbook. In ordinary
analysis we differentiate a quantity with respect to time, and by “time” we almost always mean homoge-
neous clock time 𝑡, measured in seconds — the uniformly elapsing, directionless parameter of physics. In
RTC the central discovery of the thesis is precisely the claim that the relevant independent variable for con-
sciousness and human experience is not that homogeneous clock time, but dynamic experiential time 𝜏 ,
operationalised through the percept (the perceptual succession 𝑃 ) and the Psychophysical Time Quan-
tum (PPTQ). Consciousness and experience must be differentiated with respect to the percept, not with
respect to the second hand.
This manual takes the reader from the most elementary notions (change, slope, limit) to the point where this
shift of independent variable can be made fully explicit and applied to the Kuramoto model. Along the way
all the standard differentiation rules are covered and illustrated with numerous worked examples, followed
by integral calculus and nonlinear dynamics.
1.1 The three books of Steven Strogatz as reference and source of inspiration
The applied mathematical style of the thesis — and of this manual — is deeply indebted to the work of
Steven H. Strogatz. Three of his books are an explicit reference and source of inspiration:
1. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (1994; 2nd ed. 2015). The standard textbook on dynamical
systems. Strogatz treats flows on the line, fixed points and stability, bifurcations (saddle-node, trans-
critical, pitchfork, Hopf), the logistic map and the route to chaos through period doubling, and — in
the chapter on coupled oscillators — the Kuramoto model. Part IV of this manual follows the structure
and notation of this book. Its applied differential calculus (derivatives as velocity fields, linearisation
through the Jacobian) is entirely in the service of the phenomenology of the system — exactly the
attitude RTC adopts.
2. Sync. The Emerging Science of Spontaneous Order (2003). Strogatz’s popular-science account
of synchronisation: fireflies flashing in unison, heart cells, applauding audiences, and the mathematical
core of these — the Kuramoto model and the order parameter. This book supplies the conceptual
motivation for the RTC claim that coherence is a natural, unavoidable outcome of coupled resonators,
and not something that must be imposed from outside.
3. Infinite Powers. How Calculus Reveals the Secrets of the Universe (2019). Strogatz’s
history and philosophy of calculus. The “Infinity Principle” (split a hard problem into infinitely many
infinitely small, easy pieces and add them back up), the derivative as an instantaneous rate of change,
the integral as accumulation, and the Fundamental Theorem that connects the two. Parts II and III of
this manual follow the didactic line of this book: first understand what change is, only then calculate.
Wherever a concept is introduced for the first time in this manual, a boxed note (“Strogatz reading guide”)
indicates which chapter in which book contains the extended treatment.
1.2 How to read this manual
• Part I lays down the guiding thread: the distinction between clock time 𝑡, experiential time 𝜏 and
percept index 𝑃 , and why this distinction bears on the hard problem of consciousness.
• Part II is a complete course in differential calculus: limit, derivative, and all the differentiation rules
with proofs and worked examples.
4

-- 4 of 32 --

• Part III is a course in integral calculus: the definite integral, the Fundamental Theorem, integration
techniques, and the solution of differential equations (analytic and numerical).
• Part IV applies this to the nonlinear dynamics of Chapter 9: fixed points, bifurcations, the logistic
map, oscillators and the Kuramoto model.
• Part V carries out the RTC reparametrisation: the transition 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 → 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑃 through 𝑑𝑡 = 𝜏(𝑃 ) 𝑑𝑃 , the
PPTQ-scaled Kuramoto model, and the derivation of the Mind-Energy law 𝐸𝑚 = 1/𝜏 3.
• Part VI discusses the epistemological status of all this: what the formalism does and does not prove,
and how percept differentiation contributes to the RTC treatment of the hard problem.
• Part VII contains reference tables, a list of symbols and code examples in R and Python.

2 PART I — THE GUIDING THREAD: WITH RESPECT TO
WHAT DO WE DIFFERENTIATE?
2.1 The problem of the independent variable
2.1.1 What differentiation actually does
Differentiation is the measurement of change per unit of something else. The derivative 𝑑𝑓
𝑑𝑥 answers the
question: “If 𝑥 increases by a minuscule amount, how much does 𝑓 change, per unit of 𝑥?” The choice of 𝑥
— the independent variable — is therefore not a technical detail but a substantive decision about which
change we consider important.
In physics that choice is almost always clock time 𝑡. The velocity of a particle is 𝑑𝑥
𝑑𝑡 ; the acceleration is 𝑑2𝑥
𝑑𝑡2 ;
the phase change of an oscillator is 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 . Clock time is thereby taken to be:
• homogeneous: every second equals every other second;
• directionless (in dynamics): the parameter itself contains no “now”, no flow direction;
• external: the clock runs independently of the system being described.
2.1.2 Why this is not enough for consciousness
RTC claims that lived experience is not homogeneous, not directionless and not external. The experienced
duration of an event depends on the state of consciousness: in deep meditation time “stretches”, in acute
stress it “speeds up”, in flow it “disappears”. Two clock seconds can be phenomenologically utterly unequal.
If we differentiate the dynamics of consciousness with respect to clock time, we average away precisely what
we are trying to explain.
RTC resolves this by choosing a different independent variable. Experience unfolds in discrete chunks —
percepts — each with a characteristic duration, the PPTQ 𝜏 (order of magnitude ∼ 62 ms). The succession
of percepts forms an ordered counting variable 𝑃 : percept 1, percept 2, percept 3, …. The central RTC claim
is:
The fundamental independent variable of conscious temporal dynamics is the per-
ceptual succession 𝑃 , scaled by the PPTQ 𝜏, and not the external clock time 𝑡.
Mathematically this is captured by the relation
𝑑𝑡 = 𝜏(𝑃 ) 𝑑𝑃 (1.1)
which says: one percept step (𝑑𝑃 = 1) corresponds to a clock duration of 𝜏(𝑃 ) seconds, and 𝜏 may itself de-
pend on the perceptual state 𝑃 . Everything that follows in this manual is ultimately a tool for understanding,
justifying and applying equation (1.1).
2.1.3 Three notions of time, sharply distinguished

The relation between 𝑡 and 𝑃 is not linear as soon as 𝜏 varies. That is precisely the mathematical content of
the RTC discovery.
Strogatz reading guide. The idea that the choice of independent variable determines the physics of a
problem runs as a theme through Infinite Powers (chapters 1–3: “calculus as the language of the universe”).
The idea that time in a dynamical system is a parameter that may be rescaled is the core of the “flows” in
Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, chapter 2.
2.2 The central claim and the hard problem
The hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers, 1995) is the question of why and how physical processes are
accompanied by lived experience — why “there is something it is like” to undergo a particular brain process.
The “easy” problems (attention, integration, reporting) can be described in functional or computational
terms; the “hard” problem seems to escape this.
RTC does not claim that mathematics explains away the hard problem. The ontological core — that experi-
ence is primary (Axiom I) — is a metaphysical claim, not a claim that can be proven by an equation. What
RTC does claim, and this is where this manual becomes relevant, is the following:
As soon as one differentiates the dynamics of consciousness with respect to the per-
cept 𝑃 rather than with respect to clock time 𝑡, a formal framework arises in which
the temporal organisation of experience becomes an autonomous, measurable and
falsifiable explanatory variable. The “explanatory gap” thereby shifts from an unbridge-
able mystery to a specific, quantitative model difference between a 𝑡-indexed and a 𝑃 -indexed
description.
The burden of proof that the thesis carries is therefore not “here is a proof that qualia exist”, but: “here is a
mathematically explicit, testable formulation in which the difference between physical time and experienced
time does the work, with concrete predictions (𝛽 = −3 in the Mind-Energy law; 𝑀𝑃 ≻ 𝑀𝑡 in model
comparison) that can fail.” Part VI develops this argument in full. First, however, the reader must master
the mathematics.

3 PART II — DIFFERENTIAL CALCULUS FROM THE
GROUND UP
3.1 Functions, change and slope
3.1.1 Functions
A function 𝑓 assigns to each value of an input quantity 𝑥 exactly one value 𝑓(𝑥) of an output quantity.
Examples:
• 𝑓(𝑡) = 3𝑡 + 2 — a straight line;
• 𝑔(𝑡) = 𝑡2 — a parabola;
• 𝜃(𝑡) = 𝜔𝑡 — the phase of an oscillator turning at constant angular frequency 𝜔;
• 𝜏(𝑃 ) — the PPTQ as a function of the percept index (in RTC not a constant).
3.1.2 Average rate of change
The average rate of change of 𝑓 over the interval [𝑥, 𝑥 + ℎ] is
Δ𝑓
Δ𝑥 = 𝑓(𝑥 + ℎ) − 𝑓(𝑥)
ℎ . (2.1)
Geometrically this is the slope of the chord (secant) through the points (𝑥, 𝑓(𝑥)) and (𝑥 + ℎ, 𝑓(𝑥 + ℎ)).
Worked example 2.1. Take 𝑔(𝑡) = 𝑡2, 𝑥 = 3, ℎ = 0.1:
𝑔(3.1) − 𝑔(3)
0.1 = 9.61 − 9
0.1 = 0.61
0.1 = 6.1.
With ℎ = 0.01: 9.0601 − 9
0.01 = 6.01. With ℎ = 0.001: 6.001. The values approach 6.
3.2 The limit
3.2.1 The idea
The limit lim
ℎ→0 𝐹 (ℎ) = 𝐿 means: by choosing ℎ sufficiently close to 0 (but not equal to 0) one can bring 𝐹 (ℎ)
as close to 𝐿 as desired. The limit asks about the behaviour near a point, not the value at that point — and
that is exactly what is needed, because in (2.1) substituting ℎ = 0 is forbidden (division by zero).
3.2.2 Formal definition (epsilon–delta)
lim
ℎ→0 𝐹 (ℎ) = 𝐿 if and only if: for every 𝜀 > 0 there exists a 𝛿 > 0 such that 0 < |ℎ| < 𝛿 implies |𝐹 (ℎ) − 𝐿| < 𝜀.
3.2.3 Rules for limits
If lim 𝐹 and lim 𝐺 exist, then:
• lim(𝐹 ± 𝐺) = lim 𝐹 ± lim 𝐺;
• lim(𝐹 ⋅ 𝐺) = lim 𝐹 ⋅ lim 𝐺;
• lim(𝐹 /𝐺) = lim 𝐹 / lim 𝐺 provided lim 𝐺 ≠ 0;
• lim(𝑐 ⋅ 𝐹 ) = 𝑐 ⋅ lim 𝐹 .
Worked example 2.2. Compute lim
ℎ→0
(3 + ℎ)2 − 9
ℎ . Expand the numerator: (9 + 6ℎ + ℎ2) − 9 = 6ℎ + ℎ2. So
6ℎ + ℎ2
ℎ = 6 + ℎ (ℎ ≠ 0), lim
ℎ→0(6 + ℎ) = 6.
This confirms Worked example 2.1 exactly.

3.2.4 A fundamental limit: lim
ℎ→0

ℎ = 1
(with ℎ in radians). This limit — provable geometrically via the squeeze theorem with cos ℎ ≤ sin ℎ
ℎ ≤ 1 —
is the engine behind the derivatives of sin and cos, and hence behind all oscillator dynamics.
Strogatz reading guide. Infinite Powers, chapter 4 (“Putting Limits to Work”) treats precisely this limit
and the “0/0” puzzle. The attitude “you may divide by ℎ as long as ℎ ≠ 0, and only then take the limit” is
the core of Strogatz’s Infinity Principle.
3.3 The derivative
3.3.1 Definition
The derivative of 𝑓 at 𝑥 is the limit of the chord slope as the interval shrinks to zero:
𝑓′(𝑥) = 𝑑𝑓
𝑑𝑥 = lim
ℎ→0
𝑓(𝑥 + ℎ) − 𝑓(𝑥)
ℎ . (2.2)
If this limit exists, 𝑓 is differentiable at 𝑥. Geometrically 𝑓′(𝑥) is the slope of the tangent line to the
graph at (𝑥, 𝑓(𝑥)); physically it is the instantaneous rate of change.
Notation. 𝑓′(𝑥) (Lagrange), 𝑑𝑓
𝑑𝑥 (Leibniz),	̇	 𝑓 (Newton, for the derivative with respect to time). In this
manual we use 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 for the phase change with respect to clock time and 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑃 for the phase change with respect
to percept.

3.3.3 Differentiability implies continuity
If 𝑓 is differentiable at 𝑥, then 𝑓 is continuous there. The converse does not hold: 𝑓(𝑥) = |𝑥| is continuous
at 0 but has a corner there and no derivative. This is relevant for RTC: at an abrupt state transition (for
example a sudden jump in 𝜏) the percept–time relation is continuous but not necessarily differentiable; one
then works piecewise.

3.4 All the differentiation rules
Below are the rules one needs. Each rule is given with a brief justification and at least one worked example.
A compact reference table appears at the end of the manual (Appendix A).
3.4.1 Rule 1 — The constant rule
If 𝑓(𝑥) = 𝑐 (constant), then 𝑓′(𝑥) = 0.
Reason: 𝑓(𝑥 + ℎ) − 𝑓(𝑥) = 𝑐 − 𝑐 = 0, so the difference quotient is 0.
Worked example. The intrinsic frequency 𝜔𝑖 of a Kuramoto oscillator is (per oscillator) constant: 𝑑𝜔𝑖
𝑑𝑡 = 0.
3.4.2 Rule 2 — The power rule
For every real exponent 𝑛: if 𝑓(𝑥) = 𝑥𝑛, then
𝑓′(𝑥) = 𝑛 𝑥𝑛−1. (2.3)
Reason (integer 𝑛): via the binomial expansion (𝑥+ℎ)𝑛 = 𝑥𝑛+𝑛𝑥𝑛−1ℎ+(𝑛
2)𝑥𝑛−2ℎ2+⋯; after dividing by ℎ and
letting ℎ → 0 only 𝑛𝑥𝑛−1 remains. For rational and real 𝑛 the rule follows from the exponential/logarithmic
rules (see Rule 8) together with the chain rule.
Worked examples.

If 𝑔(𝑥) = 𝑐 𝑓(𝑥), then 𝑔′(𝑥) = 𝑐 𝑓′(𝑥).

3.4.7 Rule 7 — The chain rule
This is the most important rule for this manual, because the RTC reparametrisation is an application of it.
If 𝑦 = 𝑓(𝑢) and 𝑢 = 𝑔(𝑥), then 𝑦 is a function of 𝑥 via the composition 𝑦 = 𝑓(𝑔(𝑥)), and
𝑑𝑦
𝑑𝑥 = 𝑑𝑦
𝑑𝑢 ⋅ 𝑑𝑢
𝑑𝑥 = 𝑓′(𝑔(𝑥)) ⋅ 𝑔′(𝑥). (2.6)
Reason (sketch): Δ𝑦
Δ𝑥 = Δ𝑦
Δ𝑢 ⋅ Δ𝑢
Δ𝑥 for Δ𝑢 ≠ 0; take the limit. The Leibniz notation makes the rule almost
self-evident: the “𝑑𝑢’s cancel” — a formally valid intuition as long as 𝑔′(𝑥) ≠ 0.
Worked example 2.10. 𝑑

3.5 Applications of the derivative
3.5.1 Tangent line and linear approximation
The linear approximation (first-order Taylor) of 𝑓 around 𝑥0:
𝑓(𝑥) ≈ 𝑓(𝑥0) + 𝑓′(𝑥0)(𝑥 − 𝑥0). (2.9)
This is the tool with which one linearises a nonlinear system around a fixed point (§10.3). Strogatz calls this
“the derivative as a local, linear approximation” (Infinite Powers, ch. 6).
Worked example 2.18. √101 ≈ √100 + 1
2√100 (1) = 10 + 0.05 = 10.05 (exact: 10.0499 …).
3.5.2 Extrema
At a local maximum or minimum of a differentiable function, 𝑓′(𝑥) = 0 (stationary point). The sign of 𝑓″(𝑥)
distinguishes a maximum (𝑓″ < 0) from a minimum (𝑓″ > 0).
Worked example 2.19. The Kuramoto coupling force on oscillator 𝑖 from one neighbour, 𝑔(𝜙) = 𝐾 sin 𝜙
with 𝜙 = 𝜃𝑗 − 𝜃𝑖, is maximal where 𝑔′(𝜙) = 𝐾 cos 𝜙 = 0, hence at 𝜙 = 𝜋/2: a phase difference of 90∘ produces
the strongest “pull” toward synchronisation.

4.2 The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
This theorem connects differentiation and integration as inverses of each other.
Part 1. If 𝐹 (𝑥) = ∫

In practice: to integrate, find a function whose derivative is the integrand.

4.5 Differential equations
An ordinary differential equation (ODE) relates an unknown function to its derivatives, for example
𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 = 𝜔 + 𝐾 sin(Ψ − 𝜃). To solve an ODE means: to find the function 𝜃(𝑡) that satisfies it.
4.5.1 Separation of variables
If 𝑑𝑦
𝑑𝑥 = 𝐴(𝑥) 𝐵(𝑦), then ∫ 𝑑𝑦
𝐵(𝑦) = ∫ 𝐴(𝑥) 𝑑𝑥.
Worked example 3.8 — the Adler equation (two coupled oscillators). The phase difference 𝜙 =
𝜃2 − 𝜃1 of two oscillators satisfies (see §11.2)
𝑑𝜙
𝑑𝑡 = Δ𝜔 − 𝐾 sin 𝜙.
In a locked state 𝑑𝜙
𝑑𝑡 = 0, so sin 𝜙∗ = Δ𝜔
𝐾 . This has a solution (and hence phase locking) if and only if
|Δ𝜔| ≤ 𝐾. This is Strogatz’s classic result on the synchronisation threshold (Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos,
§4.5 and §8.2; Sync, ch. 2).
4.5.2 Numerical solution: Euler’s method
𝜃(𝑡 + Δ𝑡) ≈ 𝜃(𝑡) + Δ𝑡 ⋅ 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 . (3.5)
This is nothing but the linear approximation (2.9) applied repeatedly. For better accuracy one uses Runge–
Kutta 4 (RK4).
Worked example 3.9 — Euler on one oscillator. 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 = 𝜔 with 𝜔 = 2𝜋 ⋅ 10 ≈ 62.83 rad/s (a 10 Hz alpha
oscillator), 𝜃(0) = 0, Δ𝑡 = 0.01 s. After one step: 𝜃 = 0.628 rad. After 6.2 steps (𝑡 = 0.062 s = 𝜏 ): 𝜃 ≈ 3.90
rad ≈ 223∘. Per PPTQ window the oscillator therefore turns roughly 2
3 of a full cycle.
4.5.3 Reparametrising an ODE
Given 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 = 𝑓(𝜃) and 𝑑𝑡
𝑑𝑃 = 𝜏 (𝑃 ), the chain rule gives directly the reparametrised ODE:
𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑃 = 𝜏(𝑃 ) 𝑓(𝜃). (3.6)
This is the formal basis of the PPTQ-scaled Kuramoto model (Part V). Note: the trajectory (the path 𝜃
takes) remains the same set of points; only the speed at which the path is traversed changes, and with it the
relation to the external clock.

5 PART IV — NONLINEAR DYNAMICS AND THE KU-
RAMOTO MODEL
5.1 Dynamical systems and phase space
A dynamical system is given by a state vector x(𝑡) ∈ ℝ𝑛 and a vector field	̇	 x = F(x) that at each point
prescribes the instantaneous speed and direction. The phase space is the space of all possible states; a
trajectory is a solution curve.
Examples from Chapter 9 of the thesis:
• Logistic map (discrete): 𝑥𝑛+1 = 𝑟 𝑥𝑛(1 − 𝑥𝑛) — model for reflexive amplification and the route to
chaos.
• Kuramoto model (continuous, 𝑁 -dimensional):	̇	 𝜃𝑖 = 𝜔𝑖 + 𝐾
𝑁 ∑𝑗 sin(𝜃𝑗 − 𝜃𝑖) — model for percept
formation through synchronisation.
• Ginzburg–Landau field (continuum field): 𝜕𝑡𝜓 = 𝜓 −(1+𝑖𝜔)|𝜓|2𝜓 +∇2𝜓 +𝜂 — heuristic description
of the holographic field.
5.2 Fixed points and stability
A fixed point (equilibrium) x∗ satisfies F(x∗) = 0: the system stands still there. Stability is determined
by linearisation: write x = x∗ + 𝛿, then	̇	 𝛿 ≈ 𝐽 (x∗) 𝛿 with 𝐽 the Jacobian (matrix of partial derivatives, Rule
11). The signs of the real parts of the eigenvalues of 𝐽 determine whether perturbations grow (unstable) or
decay (stable).
Worked example 4.1 — 1D.	̇	 𝑥 = 𝑓(𝑥) = 𝑟𝑥 − 𝑥3 (pitchfork normal form). Fixed points: 𝑥∗ = 0 and
(for 𝑟 > 0) 𝑥∗ = ±√𝑟. Linearisation: 𝑓′(𝑥) = 𝑟 − 3𝑥2. At 𝑥∗ = 0: 𝑓′(0) = 𝑟 — stable for 𝑟 < 0, unstable
for 𝑟 > 0. At 𝑥∗ = ±√𝑟: 𝑓′(±√𝑟) = 𝑟 − 3𝑟 = −2𝑟 < 0 — stable. At 𝑟 = 0 the number and nature of the
equilibria change: a bifurcation.
5.3 Bifurcations
A bifurcation is a qualitative change in the dynamics when a control parameter crosses a critical value. The
four standard types (Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, ch. 3 and 8):

one unstable). For 𝑟 = 0: one (semi-stable) equilibrium. For 𝑟 > 0: no equilibria — the system “escapes”.

5.4 The logistic map and the route to chaos
𝑥𝑛+1 = 𝑟 𝑥𝑛(1 − 𝑥𝑛), 𝑥𝑛 ∈ [0, 1], 𝑟 ∈ [0, 4]. (4.1)
This is equation (9.6) from the thesis. The derivative of the map is 𝑓′(𝑥) = 𝑟(1 − 2𝑥).
Fixed point. 𝑥∗ = 𝑟𝑥∗(1 − 𝑥∗) ⇒ 𝑥∗ = 0 or 𝑥∗ = 1 − 1
𝑟 .
Stability of 𝑥∗ = 1 − 1/𝑟. 𝑓′(𝑥∗) = 𝑟(1 − 2(1 − 1
𝑟 )) = 𝑟( − 1 + 2
𝑟 ) = 2 − 𝑟. Stable as long as |2 − 𝑟| < 1,
hence 1 < 𝑟 < 3. At 𝑟 = 3, |𝑓′| = 1: period doubling to a 2-cycle.
Worked example 4.3 — iteration at 𝑟 = 3.2, 𝑥0 = 0.5.
𝑛 𝑥𝑛
0 0.5000
1 3.2 ⋅ 0.5 ⋅ 0.5 = 0.8000
2 3.2 ⋅ 0.8 ⋅ 0.2 = 0.5120
3 3.2 ⋅ 0.512 ⋅ 0.488 = 0.7995
4 0.5130
5 0.7994
The system settles into a 2-cycle alternating between ≈ 0.513 and ≈ 0.799. The (formerly stable) fixed
point 𝑥∗ = 1 − 1/3.2 = 0.6875 is now unstable (𝑓′(𝑥∗) = 2 − 3.2 = −1.2, |−1.2| > 1).
The period-doubling cascade. Further increase of 𝑟 gives 4-, 8-, 16-cycles over ever shorter parameter in-
tervals, with the universal Feigenbaum constant 𝛿 ≈ 4.669 as the convergence ratio. At 𝑟∞ ≈ 3.5699 chaos
begins: sensitive dependence on initial conditions. This is Phase III in the thesis (“chaotic de-resonance”,
𝑟 > 3.57).
Strogatz reading guide. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos ch. 10 (“One-Dimensional Maps”) treats the
logistic map, the cascade and Feigenbaum universality in full.
5.5 Oscillators: phase, frequency, and the phase derivative
An oscillator is a system that runs through a cycle. Its state is summarised by a single angle, the phase
𝜃 ∈ [0, 2𝜋). The angular frequency is the phase derivative:
𝜔 = 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 .
A uniform oscillator has 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 = 𝜔 constant, so 𝜃(𝑡) = 𝜃0 + 𝜔𝑡 (integration: Worked example 3.2). The period
is 𝑇 = 2𝜋/𝜔; the ordinary frequency 𝑓 = 𝜔/2𝜋 in Hz.
Worked example 4.4. A gamma oscillator of 40 Hz: 𝜔 = 2𝜋 ⋅ 40 ≈ 251.3 rad/s, 𝑇 = 25 ms. Within one
PPTQ window of 62 ms it completes 62/25 ≈ 2.5 cycles.
5.6 Two coupled oscillators
Let 𝜃1, 𝜃2 be two oscillators with intrinsic frequencies 𝜔1, 𝜔2, sinusoidally coupled with strength 𝐾:
̇
𝜃1 = 𝜔1 + 𝐾 sin(𝜃2 − 𝜃1),̇ 𝜃2 = 𝜔2 + 𝐾 sin(𝜃1 − 𝜃2).
Define the phase difference 𝜙 = 𝜃2 − 𝜃1. Then (sum and difference rule, plus sin(−𝜙) = − sin 𝜙):
̇
𝜙 =̇ 𝜃2 −̇ 𝜃1 = (𝜔2 − 𝜔1) − 2𝐾 sin 𝜙 = Δ𝜔 − 2𝐾 sin 𝜙. (4.2)

This is the Adler equation. Phase locking (̇ 𝜙 = 0) requires sin 𝜙∗ = Δ𝜔
2𝐾 , solvable if and only if |Δ𝜔| ≤ 2𝐾.
Worked example 4.5. 𝜔1 = 2𝜋(10), 𝜔2 = 2𝜋(11) rad/s, so Δ𝜔 = 2𝜋 ≈ 6.28 rad/s. Locking requires

oscillators turn locked, with the faster one 51.7∘ ahead.

6 PART V — THE RTC REPARAMETRISATION: DIFFEREN-
TIATING OVER THE PERCEPT
Now all the threads come together. This part carries out, step by step, the transition from the classical,
clock-indexed Kuramoto model to the PPTQ-scaled, percept-indexed RTC model, and in addition derives
the Mind-Energy law 𝐸𝑚 = 1/𝜏 3 in full.
6.1 The transformation 𝑑𝑡 = 𝜏(𝑃 ) 𝑑𝑃
6.1.1 Motivation
In the classical model 𝑡 (seconds) is the independent variable. RTC claims: conscious experience unfolds in
percepts, discrete integration windows. Number them 𝑃 = 1, 2, 3, … Each percept spans a clock duration
equal to the PPTQ 𝜏 of that moment. The infinitesimal version of this is:
𝑑𝑡 = 𝜏(𝑃 ) 𝑑𝑃 (5.1)
𝜏(𝑃 ) is dynamic: it depends on the state of consciousness, which itself evolves with 𝑃 . The empirically
expected ordering is
𝜏meditation > 𝜏waking > 𝜏stress. (5.2)
6.1.2 Epistemic status of (5.1)
As the project notes emphasise: (5.1) is not a pure mathematical identity unless 𝑃 is explicitly defined as a
dimensionless percept-count variable. We do so here: 𝑃 counts percepts, [𝑃 ] = 1, and 𝜏 carries the unit
second. Under that definition (5.1) is a modelling assumption with content: it claims that the natural “tick”
of conscious dynamics is the percept, not the second. Precisely because it is an assumption with content, it
is testable (Part VI).

𝑑𝑡 to 𝑑𝜃

6.2.1 What changes mathematically, and what does not?
• The set of trajectories in phase space remains identical: (5.4) traverses the same curves as (4.3),
because the factor 𝜏(𝑃 ) > 0 rescales only the speed, not the direction of the vector field (§3.6).
• The relation to the external clock does change: where 𝜏 is large (meditation), less perceptual
change happens per clock second; where 𝜏 is small (stress), more.
• The coherence build-up per percept becomes: 𝑑𝑅
𝑑𝑃 = 𝜏(𝑃 )⋅ 𝑑𝑅
𝑑𝑡 . At short 𝜏 the system accumulates
less coherence per percept — a concrete prediction about how percept formation degrades under stress.

3.90 𝑃 . After 10 percepts: 𝜃 = 39.0 rad ≈ 6.2 full revolutions. In clock time: 10 percepts = 0.62 s, and
𝜔𝑡 = 62.83 ⋅ 0.62 = 38.96 rad — consistent (the small difference is rounding).

or 𝛽 > 0 would refute the law. This is the direct statistical test criterion (see §12.5 and Part VI).

7 PART VI — EPISTEMOLOGICAL ACCOUNTABILITY AND
THE HARD PROBLEM
7.1 Four levels, sharply separated
RTC distinguishes four levels, and the strength of the formalism depends on not conflating them:
1. Ontological level. Experience is primary (Axiom I); temporal organisation is constitutive of experi-
ence. This is a metaphysical commitment; no experiment establishes it directly.
2. Formal level. 𝜏 becomes a formal variable; the relations 𝐸𝑚 ∝ 𝜏 −3 and 𝑑𝜃𝑖
𝑑𝑃 ∝ 𝜏 impose structure.
3. Operational level. 𝜏 is defined as “the characteristic temporal interval over which successive
perceptual states are integrated into a unitary experiential event”, and estimated psychophysi-
cally (temporal-order judgments, simultaneity judgments, temporal numerosity, backward masking,
temporal-integration paradigms).
4. Empirical level. Only here does the theory become vulnerable to refutation.
The formalism does not prove the axioms. It converts them into a structured set of empirical consequences.
7.2 The status of the mathematical layers (Chapter 9)
Layer Status Function
Ginzburg–Landau field theory heuristic holographic field, phase
transitions
Kuramoto synchronisation formal + computational percept formation, coherence
Bayesian inference formal perceptual updating
Nonlinear dynamics heuristic + computational attractor landscapes, bifurcations,
psychopathology
Formal = deductive proof from accepted premises; computational = simulation validation; heuristic = struc-
tural analogy without literal physical identification. This modesty forestalls the classic error — mistaking
analogy for proof — that has discredited many a formalisation in consciousness studies.
7.3 Why percept differentiation addresses the hard problem
The argument, explicit and step by step:
1. The explanatory gap, in its usual formulation, is bound to clock time. Standard theories
describe neural processes as 𝑑(⋅)
𝑑𝑡 — evolving in homogeneous external time. In that framework there is
no place for the lived temporal structure; it is averaged away. The “what it is like to experience” then
has no formal carrier.
2. RTC introduces a second, psychophysically defined temporal variable. Through 𝑑(⋅)
𝑑𝑃 with
𝑑𝑡 = 𝜏(𝑃 ) 𝑑𝑃 , the temporal organisation of experience acquires its own explicit formal carrier — 𝜏 (𝑃 )
— that is empirically distinguishable from 𝑡.
3. The shift makes the gap testable instead of mysterious. The question “how does experience
relate to physics?” is reformulated as: “Does a 𝑃 -indexed (PPTQ-scaled) description explain the
dynamics of conscious states better than a purely 𝑡-indexed description, after correcting for arousal,
sensory input and overall neural power?” Formally: compare model 𝑀𝑃 (equation 5.4) with model 𝑀𝑡
(equation 4.3) in out-of-sample prediction. RTC predicts 𝑀𝑃 ≻ 𝑀𝑡.
4. If 𝑀𝑃 ≻ 𝑀𝑡 holds up robustly, then the temporal organisation of experience is an au-
tonomous explanatory variable — not reducible to clock physics. That is the “mathematical
26

-- 26 of 32 --

burden of proof” the thesis carries: not a proof that qualia exist, but an explicit, falsifiable formalism
in which the distinction between physical time and experienced time does the explanatory work.
5. What it does not claim. It does not demonstrate that consciousness is identical to PPTQ, nor
that resonance is ontologically fundamental. It opens a route by which those ontological claims acquire
empirical consequences.
7.4 Falsifiability: the concrete criteria
• Mind-Energy law. ln 𝐸𝑚 = 𝛼 − 3 ln 𝜏 + 𝜖. Test 𝐻0 ∶ 𝛽 ≠ −3 against 𝐻1 ∶ 𝛽 = −3. A Bayesian model
comparison of 𝑀1 ∶ 𝛽 = −3 against an unconstrained power-law model 𝑀2 ∶ 𝐸𝑚 = 𝑎𝜏 𝛽 prevents an
arbitrary power law from counting as “support”.
• PPTQ-Kuramoto hypothesis. If clock-indexed dynamics consistently give better predictions of
perceptual and conscious-state transitions than PPTQ-indexed dynamics, the RTC modification loses
its justification.
• Avoiding circularity. 𝜏 must be estimated psychophysically, while Mind-Energy and neural synchro-
nisation are measured independently (EEG/MEG). Otherwise the test is not independent.
7.5 The epistemological transition summarised
metaphysical axiom → mathematical formalisation → operational definition → empirical prediction → falsifiable test.
Without this chain, RTC remains an ontological interpretation of consciousness. With it, RTC becomes
a candidate scientific theory whose central claims can be confronted with data, compared with competing
models, and rejected if its quantitative predictions fail.

8.4 Appendix D — Code examples
8.4.1 D.1 — Kuramoto (classical), R
kuramoto <- function(N = 50, K = 2.0, dt = 0.01, steps = 2000, sd_omega = 0.5) {
omega <- rnorm(N, 0, sd_omega)
theta <- runif(N, 0, 2 * pi)
R_hist <- numeric(steps)
for (s in seq_len(steps)) {
z <- mean(exp(1i * theta)) # complex order parameter
R <- Mod(z); Psi <- Arg(z)
dtheta <- omega + K * R * sin(Psi - theta) # mean-field form
theta <- theta + dt * dtheta
R_hist[s] <- R
}
R_hist
}
plot(kuramoto(K = 2.0), type = "l", ylim = c(0, 1),
xlab = "iteration", ylab = "order parameter R")
8.4.2 D.2 — RTC Kuramoto (percept-indexed) with dynamic PPTQ, Python
import numpy as np
def tau_of_P(P):
# PPTQ recovers from 43 ms (stress) toward 62 ms (waking)
return 0.062 * (1 - 0.3 * np.exp(-P / 5.0))
def rtc_kuramoto(N=50, K=2.0, dP=0.05, steps=4000, sd_omega=0.5, seed=0):
29

-- 29 of 32 --

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
omega = rng.normal(0.0, sd_omega, N)
theta = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, N)
R_hist, P = [], 0.0
for _ in range(steps):
z = np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))
R, Psi = np.abs(z), np.angle(z)
tau = tau_of_P(P)
dtheta = tau * (omega + K * R * np.sin(Psi - theta)) # equation (5.5)
theta += dP * dtheta
P += dP
R_hist.append(R)
return np.array(R_hist)
8.4.3 D.3 — Mind-Energy law and log–log check, R
tau <- c(0.100, 0.080, 0.062, 0.050, 0.042) # PPTQ per state (s)
Em <- 1 / tau^3 # equation (5.11)
fit <- lm(log(Em) ~ log(tau))
coef(fit)[["log(tau)"]] # expected: -3
8.4.4 D.4 — Logistic map, iteration, R
logistic_iter <- function(r, x0 = 0.5, n = 40) {
x <- numeric(n + 1); x[1] <- x0
for (i in seq_len(n)) x[i + 1] <- r * x[i] * (1 - x[i])
x
}
tail(logistic_iter(r = 3.2), 6) # settles into a 2-cycle ~0.513 / ~0.799

9 Closing note
This manual has sought to demonstrate one thing: that the mathematical core of The Resonating Self — the
differentiation of conscious dynamics with respect to the percept rather than with respect to clock time
— can be built up entirely from the standard tools of calculus, with no mathematical tricks and no hidden
assumptions. The chain rule (Rule 7) supplies the transition 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑡 → 𝑑𝜃
𝑑𝑃 ; the relation 𝑑𝑡 = 𝜏(𝑃 ) 𝑑𝑃 is an
explicit, testable modelling assumption; the power rule (Rule 2) supplies the Mind-Energy law 𝐸𝑚 = 𝜏 −3
with its falsifiable exponent 𝛽 = −3.
What remains is not a proof that the hard problem has been solved in the sense that the mystery has vanished.
What remains is a formalism in which the distinction between physical and experienced time performs the
explanatory work, with predictions that can fail. In the spirit of Strogatz: calculus does not reveal why there
is experience, but it does give us the language to say precisely what changes, with respect to what, and how
fast — and that is the precondition for any science of consciousness worthy of the name.
32
